sourceNotes: Seeded from ASM roleplay performance indicators and marketing cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: ASM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the marketing cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: Total labor sales divided by the flat-rate hours actually billed, which lands below the posted retail rate once discounts, coupons, warranty time and internal work are blended in.
terms.whyItMatters: A service-manager roleplay that asks why gross is down when the door rate just went up is solved by showing the effective rate fell — the judge wants the division, not the posted rate.

terms.definition: The posted retail price for one hour of labor on the service-drive sign, before any coupon, menu discount, fleet agreement or warranty schedule pulls the realized rate down.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing roleplays hand you a rate increase to justify; the winning answer prices off the door rate but forecasts gross off the effective rate, because raising one does not raise the other one-for-one.

terms.definition: Flat-rate hours produced divided by clock hours actually worked on the floor — a tech who bills 9.0 hours in an 8-hour shift runs 112%, and anything over 100% is the shop's labor gross engine.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item gives hours flagged and hours worked and asks for efficiency; picking the wrong denominator gives you productivity instead and the answer is wrong.

terms.definition: Clock hours actually spent on repair orders divided by the hours the technician was paid to be available, so it measures how much of the shift the dispatcher managed to fill, not how fast the work went.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay says techs are fast but the shop misses its hours target, productivity is the number to fix — the answer is dispatching and appointment load, not paying for speed.

terms.definition: A unit of billed labor set by the manufacturer's or an independent time guide rather than by the clock, so a job published at 2.4 bills 2.4 whether it took 1.5 hours or four.
terms.whyItMatters: Every service-drive gross calculation on the exam multiplies flat-rate hours by a labor rate, and a competitor who bills clock time instead misstates both the estimate and the tech's pay.

terms.definition: Total flat-rate hours sold divided by the number of repair orders closed, the single lever that grows labor gross without more cars — moving 1.8 to 2.1 on 900 ROs sells 270 extra hours.
terms.whyItMatters: A fixed-operations roleplay judged on growing revenue with the same traffic wants this metric raised through inspection and upsell, not a rate increase.

terms.definition: Hours a service stall is occupied divided by the hours it was open and staffed, where the denominator is bays multiplied by open hours — eight bays over a nine-hour day is 72 available hours, not eight.
terms.whyItMatters: Capacity roleplays ask whether to add a bay or add a shift; computing utilization first shows whether the constraint is physical space or unfilled appointment slots.

terms.definition: A tiered pricing schedule that applies a shrinking percentage as replacement-part cost climbs — a $4 part may be priced at cost times 2.4 while a $600 part is priced at cost times 1.25.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a parts cost and the tier table, the exam expects the right band chosen and the retail computed; using one flat markup for every part overprices small items and kills the big-ticket sale.

terms.definition: Customer-pay parts sales divided by customer-pay labor sales on the same repair orders, benchmarked near 0.8 to 1.0 — a ratio far under it says technicians are diagnosing but not replacing.
terms.whyItMatters: In a fixed-operations analysis roleplay the ratio pins the shortfall on one department, telling you whether to coach the advisers or fix parts availability.

terms.definition: Combined parts and service gross profit divided by the dealership's total fixed overhead, so 100% means the back end alone pays every light bill and salary before a single car is sold.
terms.whyItMatters: A dealer-principal roleplay that asks how the store survives a slow sales month is answered with this percentage — the target is 100% and most stores run 60–80%.

terms.definition: Repair orders returning for the same complaint within a set window, usually 30 days, divided by total ROs closed — every one costs the labor twice while billing it once.
terms.whyItMatters: A quality roleplay judged on retention needs the rate computed and the cost of rework quantified, because a 3% comeback rate on 900 ROs is 27 jobs paid for out of gross.

terms.definition: The share of labor hours billed to the vehicle owner versus billed to the manufacturer, which matters because warranty work reimburses at a lower published time and rate and therefore dilutes gross per hour.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay reports rising hours but flat gross, the mix has shifted toward warranty; the fix is customer-pay marketing to older vehicles, not more technicians.

terms.definition: The manufacturer's published repair time for a covered job, typically set below the retail flat-rate time for the identical operation, and the only time a factory claim will pay regardless of what the guide shows.
terms.whyItMatters: Estimating a warranty job at retail time overstates the claim and triggers a chargeback in audit — the exam tests that the two time schedules are different numbers for the same repair.

terms.definition: The manufacturer's deadline — commonly 30 days from the repair date — inside which a completed claim must be filed, after which the dealer eats the parts and labor entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: A warranty-administration roleplay about an aging claims queue is scored on knowing the deadline and the chargeback consequence, not on generally urging faster paperwork.

terms.definition: The dollar ceiling a service manager may approve out of policy on an expired or ineligible repair before the district or zone representative must sign off — often a few hundred dollars per vehicle.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay hands you an angry owner just past warranty; the strong answer names the limit, covers what fits inside it and escalates the rest instead of promising a free repair.

terms.definition: Vehicles actually remedied divided by the population covered by a safety campaign, reported quarterly to NHTSA for eight quarters, with rates on older campaigns routinely stalling near 70%.
terms.whyItMatters: A campaign-management roleplay is judged on lifting a measurable percentage through VIN-list outreach, so the metric and its reporting duty have to be named.

terms.definition: The state-set trigger for a refund or replacement, in most states four unsuccessful attempts at the same substantial defect, or 30 cumulative days out of service, inside the warranty term or first 12–24 months.
terms.whyItMatters: A complaint roleplay where the same fault returns a third time turns on counting attempts against the threshold — the answer is to escalate before the fourth, not to keep repairing.

terms.definition: The FTC-mandated window form on every used vehicle offered for sale, declaring As Is or the warranty's exact percentage of parts and labor covered, and its terms override any contrary clause in the sales contract.
terms.whyItMatters: A used-vehicle roleplay about a dispute over a post-sale repair is decided by the posted form, so the competitor must know it controls the contract rather than the other way round.

terms.definition: The state-law cap on exceeding a written estimate without new consent, commonly 10% or a fixed dollar amount, above which the shop must reach the customer and log the approval before continuing.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay has a technician finding extra damage mid-job, the scored move is stopping at the limit and documenting fresh authorization, because unauthorized work is often uncollectable.

terms.definition: The federal Truth in Mileage Act transfer certification of mileage and its accuracy, required on title assignment but exempt for vehicles over 16,000 pounds and, under the current rule, older than 20 model years.
terms.whyItMatters: A wholesale or trade-in roleplay tests whether the competitor knows a mileage misstatement is a federal violation with treble damages, not a paperwork slip.

terms.definition: The point at which a state brands a vehicle unrepairable-or-rebuilt, typically when estimated repair cost reaches 70–80% of pre-loss actual cash value, and the brand follows the VIN permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: An appraisal roleplay is scored on comparing the repair estimate to that percentage of value before promising a resale price, since a branded title cuts trade value sharply.

terms.definition: A statutory right in most states for a dealer to force the factory to pay warranty labor and parts at retail, proved by submitting a run of consecutive qualifying customer-pay repair orders — often 100 in a row or 90 days' worth.
terms.whyItMatters: A fixed-operations roleplay about warranty gross dilution is won by naming this filing and the sequential-RO evidence, which recovers dollars no pricing change can.

terms.definition: Inventory value divided by average daily cost of parts sold, benchmarked at roughly 45–60 days, with anything unsold for twelve months counted as obsolescence against the pad.
terms.whyItMatters: An inventory roleplay must choose between stocking depth and cash tied up; the days figure decides it, and the twelve-month line decides what gets returned on the annual stock order.

terms.definition: The mandatory repair-order narrative — complaint in the customer's words, cause found by diagnosis, correction actually performed — and a claim missing any one of the three fails a factory audit.
terms.whyItMatters: Documentation roleplays and warranty-audit scenarios expect the competitor to name all three parts and explain that vague wording is what gets a paid claim charged back.

terms.definition: The standardized identifier attached to each line of a repair order that fixes the published time, the pay and the warranty eligibility for that job, so mis-coding changes what the claim pays.
terms.whyItMatters: A service-writer roleplay about inconsistent pricing between advisers is traced to coding the same job differently, which the exam expects named rather than described as sloppiness.

terms.definition: The parts, service and body departments taken together, called fixed because their overhead persists whether or not a single vehicle is sold, which is why their gross is measured against total store expense.
terms.whyItMatters: A dealership-structure roleplay asks where stable profit comes from in a down sales market, and the answer has to distinguish these departments from the variable sales side.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: The number of weeks it takes a campaign's carried-over effect to fall to 50% of its starting level, computed from the weekly retention rate as ln(0.5) ÷ ln(rate) — a rate of 0.7 gives about 1.9 weeks — so a short half-life forces flights roughly monthly while a long one permits long gaps between bursts.
terms.whyItMatters: Flighting-versus-continuity items expect the weeks figure computed, not a description of the trade-off, and the same number sets the measurement window a plan claims when it attributes sales to a campaign.

terms.definition: Holds that a firm should satisfy its target market's wants profitably only in ways that also preserve long-run consumer and social welfare — the third test the plain marketing concept leaves out — so an offering that customers genuinely want and the company profits from can still fail this standard because of the harm it does over time.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics questions that pit a profitable, popular product against a long-term harm are answered by naming this third test rather than by choosing between customers and profit.

terms.definition: The share of each ADDITIONAL dollar of after-tax income a household spends rather than saves, computed as the change in consumption divided by the change in income. It always pairs with the marginal propensity to save, and the two sum to 1 — so an MPC of 0.75 implies an MPS of 0.25.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give a household's income increase and its spending increase want this ratio, which then feeds the spending multiplier; using average spending out of total income instead of the change is the classic error.

terms.definition: A prize promotion decided by judged ability — an essay, a photo, a recipe — rather than by random draw, which removes the chance element of an illegal lottery and is the only reason it may lawfully require a purchase, where a chance-based sweepstakes must offer free entry instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay client insists that entrants buy something first, this is the structure that makes it legal, and knowing which element each format removes is what turns a vague warning into usable advice.

terms.definition: Temporary transfer of possession of personal property without any transfer of ownership — a coat check, a car left for repair, goods held in a public warehouse. The standard of care owed by the holder scales with who benefits: slight care when only the owner benefits, ordinary care when both do, and great care when only the holder benefits.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-business roleplays about a customer vehicle damaged overnight test what duty the shop owed while it sat on the lot.

terms.definition: In speech act theory (Austin and Searle), the action a speaker performs in saying something - promising, ordering, warning, refusing - as distinct from the locutionary act, which is the literal words and their sense, and the perlocutionary act, which is the effect actually produced in the hearer. 'It is cold in here' is locutionally a remark about temperature, illocutionarily a request, and perlocutionarily successful only if somebody closes the window.
terms.whyItMatters: A service roleplay in which the customer says 'I have been waiting a while' is scored on whether you answer the request rather than the sentence.

terms.definition: Helping customers make purchase decisions through planned communication.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling vocabulary supports recommendations about staff, service, and revenue.

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.definition: The distance between the top-down number corporate assumes and the sum of the territory-level bottom-up forecasts, stated as a percentage of the top-down total; a gap past roughly 5% has to be closed by named actions with volume attached to each before the plan is approved, never by splitting the difference.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-approval scenarios hand a corporate target and the field's rolled-up total and expect the gap quantified and assigned; the judge's follow-up is always which specific actions close it and what each is worth.

terms.definition: Invitations sent per existing user multiplied by the share of those invitations that convert into new users — 5 invites at a 25% conversion rate gives k = 1.25 — where any value above 1.0 compounds into self-sustaining growth and any value below 1.0 produces a decaying series that halts on its own once paid acquisition stops, so the threshold is exactly 1.0 and not merely 'high'.
terms.whyItMatters: A referral-program roleplay is scored on stating the break-even threshold and the two inputs you would change to reach it, not on calling the campaign shareable.

terms.definition: Gable's strongest of four ways to answer someone's good news, formed by crossing active with passive and constructive with destructive: responding actively and constructively means asking questions that let the person relive the event, while passive-constructive is a flat nice job, active-destructive points out the downside, and passive-destructive changes the subject. Only the first strengthens the relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays on recognizing a team member's contribution are scored on a specific, curious response in the moment rather than a generic congratulation or a deferred award.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by (1 − MPC), so an economy whose households spend 80 cents of each extra dollar turns $10 billion of new government purchases into as much as $50 billion of added output. The tax multiplier is always smaller, because the first dollar of a tax cut is partly saved before any of it is spent.
terms.whyItMatters: A macro item that supplies an MPC and a spending figure is asking for this computation; the tax-cut version of the same question uses a smaller multiplier and is where competitors lose points.

terms.definition: An objective-setting standard requiring an advertising goal to name a measurable communication task, a defined audience, a starting benchmark and a deadline — raise unaided awareness among women 18 to 34 from 20% to 45% within six months — rather than a sales target that advertising alone cannot own.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotional-plan roleplays are frequently scored on whether the stated objective is measurable; a competitor who promises to increase sales has written a goal that no post-campaign study can grade.

terms.definition: A sentence that does not describe an act but carries it out, so it cannot be true or false - only successful or void: 'I accept your offer,' 'I resign,' 'I hereby order 500 units.' Austin's felicity conditions are what make it stick - the right person, the right circumstances, the right form - which is why a casually typed 'agreed' from an authorized employee can create a binding acceptance while a long email full of enthusiasm creates nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-risk items that ask how a staff member bound the company in a chat message turn on this distinction between describing and doing.

terms.definition: Deals won divided by every qualified opportunity worked in the period — 15 wins out of 60 qualified opportunities is 25%. The denominator keeps opportunities that are still open or that ended in no decision, which is exactly what win rate throws out, so this figure always reads lower than win rate for the same rep.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales-management roleplay that asks you to diagnose a rep whose revenue is falling, a dropping close rate against a steady win rate points at unqualified prospecting rather than weak closing technique.

terms.definition: Ranking complaint categories by volume and cutting where the cumulative share crosses about 80% — if billing errors, late delivery and wrong item are 82% of 1,000 complaints, the remaining eleven categories split 18% and wait. Because it sorts on frequency alone, a rare category that costs the most per case needs a severity weight before it is set aside.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay handing over a year of complaint data expects the vital few named and the severity caveat stated out loud.

terms.definition: Total monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income, the figure a lender uses to decide how much more a borrower can carry.
terms.whyItMatters: Loan-approval scenarios turn on this number, and competitors are expected to compute it from a client's payment list rather than judge the debt total by feel.

terms.definition: The spending level on a diminishing-returns response curve where the last dollar invested returns exactly one dollar of contribution; below it more spending still adds profit, above it volume keeps climbing while profit falls, so the stopping test is marginal contribution per marginal dollar equal to 1.0 — not whether total return is still positive.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget items deliberately show total return positive at every spending level to see whether the competitor stops at the marginal break-even; a plan arguing for more spend past that point is refuted with its own numbers.

terms.definition: Environmental marketing claims the seller cannot substantiate, policed in the United States by the FTC's Green Guides at 16 CFR Part 260, which treat unqualified general claims such as 'eco-friendly' or 'green' as deceptive because they imply every possible environmental benefit, and require a degradability claim to mean complete breakdown within one year of customary disposal; a truthful narrow claim must therefore be stated narrowly to be lawful.
terms.whyItMatters: Sustainability roleplays that ask you to approve a packaging claim are scored on naming the standard and qualifying the claim, since an unqualified benefit statement is a legal exposure, not just a marketing choice.

terms.definition: Totals a nation's output as C + I + G + (X − M) — consumption plus business investment plus government purchases plus net exports. Imports are SUBTRACTED because they were produced abroad but already counted inside C, I and G, which is why a widening trade deficit mechanically lowers the measured figure.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP items hand you four spending categories and expect the sum with imports netted out; adding imports in, or counting government transfer payments as G, are the two ways competitors miss it.

terms.definition: Communication that informs, persuades, and reminds customers about offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion choices must fit the audience, message, and budget.

terms.definition: Brown and Levinson's term for any move that damages a hearer's public self-image - a criticism, a refusal, an order, a correction - together with the two repairs speakers use on it. Negative politeness protects the hearer's freedom by hedging and leaving an exit ('if you have a moment, could you possibly...'); positive politeness protects the hearer's need to be liked, using shared identity, praise and in-group language. Choosing the wrong repair is why a technically polite email still lands badly.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervisor roleplay that asks you to correct an employee's work is scored on which softening strategy you choose, not just on the accuracy of the correction.

terms.definition: Protects workers aged 40 and over at employers with 20 or more employees, so a 38-year-old passed over for a 55-year-old has no claim under it and neither does a 12-person shop. Unlike Title VII, it protects only the older side of the line, meaning favoring a 60-year-old over a 45-year-old is not unlawful even though both are inside the protected class.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring-decision roleplay that mentions a candidate's age needs the 40-and-over line and the 20-employee threshold before you can say whether the statute even applies.

terms.definition: The structured steps that move a customer from awareness to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the process helps competitors execute each stage well.

terms.definition: A four-step frontline script — listen without interrupting, apologize for the impact rather than admitting fault, solve inside the agent's own authority, thank the customer for reporting it. It ends at the individual fix, whereas the HEARD sequence appends a diagnose step that pushes the cause back into the process, so LAST alone leaves the failure free to recur.
terms.whyItMatters: A difficult-customer roleplay is scored step by step, and the absent diagnose step is what separates a passing recovery from a winning one.

terms.definition: The percentage volume increase a discount must produce merely to hold contribution flat: discount per unit ÷ (normal contribution per unit − discount per unit). A $1 cut against $4 of unit contribution needs 33% more units; a $2 cut against the same $4 needs 100%, which is why deep cuts almost never pay for themselves.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-approval questions give margin and discount depth and expect the required lift computed and compared with the forecast lift; anything forecast below the break-even figure is a promotion the plan should reject.

terms.definition: The process of creating, communicating, and delivering value to customers.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the umbrella concept behind many cluster and roleplay decisions.

terms.definition: A general, ongoing rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of money.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation affects demand, business costs, and pricing strategy.

terms.definition: Documents and files that capture a business's transactions, operations, and decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Accurate records are required for compliance, accountability, and historical reference.

terms.definition: Reach multiplied by average frequency, the one number that sizes a schedule's total weight: 40% of the target seen four times is 160. The same 160 can be bought as 80% reach at 2.0 frequency, which is why the figure alone never describes a schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-planning items hand the competitor a reach figure and a frequency figure and ask for the schedule's weight, or give the weight and one factor and ask for the other; a roleplay defending a media plan to a client is expected to state both halves, not just the total.

terms.definition: The reasoning error of treating sequence as cause: sales rose after the new sign went up, therefore the sign raised sales. The test has two parts - could any other change explain the same movement (season, a competitor closing, a price cut, a general market lift), and is there a mechanism connecting the two? It is the fallacy behind most claimed advertising results, because campaigns are launched in the same weeks that demand naturally climbs.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that hands you a sales bump right after a campaign is scored on whether you ask for a control comparison instead of claiming the credit.

terms.definition: Deals won divided only by the deals that reached a final decision — wins plus losses — so 15 wins among 45 resolved deals is 33%, with open and no-decision opportunities excluded from the denominator entirely. That narrower denominator is the whole difference from close rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that hand you a pipeline table expect you to notice which opportunities belong in the denominator; counting still-open deals as losses is the single most common wrong answer.

terms.definition: Hear, empathize, apologize, resolve, diagnose — five steps whose last one is the whole difference: once the customer is satisfied the employee traces why the failure happened and reports it, converting a single complaint into a process fix. The four-step LAST script stops at resolve and generates no such feedback into the operation.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about a failure that keeps recurring reward the competitor who closes the loop rather than just the ticket.

terms.definition: Period sales divided by that period's seasonal index — 130,000 units in a month carrying an index of 1.30 is 100,000 on a level basis — and any trend line must be fitted to these adjusted figures, because fitting a line straight to raw seasonal data reads the busy season as growth that is not there.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast items hand monthly actuals alongside indexes and expect the adjusted series produced before any projection; skipping the division is the standard error that inflates a plan's growth claim and gets caught on the follow-up.

terms.definition: Summing durations along every dependency chain and taking the longest one as the shortest possible project duration; every task on it has zero float, so any slip there slips the whole project, while a delay off it is absorbed.
terms.whyItMatters: A project roleplay that asks which of several late tasks to escalate is answered by locating the zero-float chain, because effort spent on the others buys no finish-date improvement.

terms.definition: Value created by converting raw materials into a finished good a buyer actually wants — wheat into bread, bauxite into a can — as distinct from place utility (moving the good to where the buyer shops), time utility (having it on hand at the hour demand occurs), and possession utility (transferring ownership through payment terms); a redesign adds form utility, a faster truck does not.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that ask how marketing adds value to a product are scored on naming which of the four utilities each activity creates and separating them; a general answer about 'adding value' loses the point.

terms.definition: Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100 — a price index covering every good and service an economy produces. Unlike the consumer price index it uses no fixed basket, so its weights shift automatically as spending patterns change, and it excludes imported goods that the CPI includes.
terms.whyItMatters: An item giving nominal and real GDP for the same year is asking for this ratio, and an item asking which price measure covers the whole economy rather than a household basket is asking for it by name.

terms.definition: The blend of advertising, publicity, sales promotion, and personal selling.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix lets competitors recommend more than one communication path.

terms.definition: The motion in Robert's Rules that closes debate and forces an immediate vote on the pending item. It is not the item itself and it is not a question: it must be seconded, is undebatable and unamendable, and takes a two-thirds vote because it strips members of the right to speak. Someone shouting 'Question!' from the floor has not made this motion and has not ended debate - the chair must still put it to the assembly.
terms.whyItMatters: A meeting-procedure item that shows a chair cutting off discussion on a simple majority is testing the two-thirds threshold attached to this motion.

terms.definition: Identifying and qualifying potential customers who may need an offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective prospecting builds the foundation for successful sales.

terms.definition: Credential a private board grants after a psychometrically validated exam and keeps alive through periodic recertification, evidencing tested competence rather than legal permission. A certificate of completion is the near-neighbor that fools students: it is awarded merely for finishing a course, is never re-earned, and no board can revoke it.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on career-advancement resources ask which credential an employer will actually pay for; the answer is the one with an exam and a renewal cycle behind it.

terms.definition: An advance promise of a specific payout when a stated service standard is missed — the meal free after 30 minutes, the night comped on a late check-in — paid on the condition alone with no proof of loss and no argument. A warranty answers a product defect after the fact and requires a claim to be substantiated; this one is designed to be trivially easy to invoke.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a competitor who proposes an unconditional, easy-to-claim guarantee for a service failure instead of extending a warranty that does not apply.

terms.definition: Divides a town's retail sales per resident by the state's retail sales per resident: 1.00 means locals spend exactly the statewide average at home, above 1.00 means the town is pulling shoppers in from outside its borders, and 0.80 means a fifth of local buying power is leaking to other towns.
terms.whyItMatters: Trading-area and site questions give local and statewide sales per person and expect the ratio plus a read on leakage; it is the figure behind arguing that a market is under-served and can support another store.

terms.definition: Intangible activities that satisfy customer needs and wants.
terms.whyItMatters: Services require different quality, staffing, and marketing choices than goods.

terms.definition: The short-run inverse trade-off between inflation and unemployment: driving unemployment below the natural rate buys fewer jobless at the price of faster inflation. The long-run version is vertical at the natural rate, so once workers build the higher inflation into their expectations the trade-off disappears and only the inflation remains.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask what a central bank gives up when it stimulates an economy already at full employment; the long-run vertical version is what explains why the 1970s tried to buy jobs and got stagflation instead.

terms.definition: Rating points counted only against the demographic actually being bought instead of against every household in the market, so a broad-appeal buy delivering 200 gross rating points may deliver just 60 of these if only 30% of its viewers fall inside the target.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows a schedule looking strong on total weight but thin on the buying demographic is testing this distinction, and a media-plan roleplay that quotes only the gross figure to a client buying an 18-to-34 audience has hidden the waste.

terms.definition: Taking ownership of an adjacent stage of a firm's own supply chain — backward toward suppliers or forward toward distribution and retail — which is distinct from horizontal integration, the acquisition of a competitor at the same stage that buys market share rather than supply control.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a coffee chain buys its own roasting plant is scored on naming backward vertical integration and its margin and risk consequences, not just 'buying a supplier'.

terms.definition: A member's assertion that the rules are being broken at this moment - a motion made out of order, debate wandering off the pending question, a vote miscounted. It may interrupt a speaker, requires no second, is not debatable, and is settled by the chair's ruling rather than a vote, though any two members may appeal that ruling to the assembly. It must be timely: raised after the offending action is complete, it is normally too late.
terms.whyItMatters: Chapter meetings and management roleplays run on a written agenda test whether you know which objections may interrupt a speaker and which must wait for the floor.

terms.definition: Open opportunity value divided by the quota for the period: $900,000 of open deals against a $300,000 quota is 3x, the usual rule of thumb for a team that wins about one deal in three. Coverage below the reciprocal of the win rate means the quota is arithmetically unreachable no matter how well the rep sells.
terms.whyItMatters: A district-manager roleplay judged on forecasting expects you to test coverage before promising a number, and to prescribe prospecting rather than closing coaching when coverage is thin.

terms.term: Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
terms.definition: An FTC rule under which a seller advertising no shipping date must ship within 30 days of a properly completed order, or send the buyer a revised date carrying the right to cancel for a prompt refund. Staying silent past the deadline obliges a refund whether or not the customer asks, so the clock runs against the seller by default.
terms.whyItMatters: An online-order complaint roleplay is decided by this clock, and the winning answer is a legal duty rather than a courtesy gesture.

terms.definition: Compares an industry's share of local employment or sales with its share nationally — local share ÷ national share — so 1.0 marks a perfectly typical market, above about 1.25 says the activity is concentrated here and likely serves customers beyond it, and below about 0.75 says local demand is being met from somewhere else.
terms.whyItMatters: Situation-analysis questions supply local and national employment figures and expect the ratio read against 1.0; it is how a plan defends choosing one metro over another with evidence rather than preference.

terms.definition: Value added by making ownership transferable — credit terms, layaway, financing, leasing, the transaction mechanics themselves — rather than by making the good (form utility), delivering it to the buyer's location (place utility), or holding it until demand appears (time utility); a dealer that adds 60-month zero-interest financing changes the product's form, place, and time not at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and finance roleplays that ask you to justify offering a payment plan want the answer framed as a marketing utility the firm creates, not as a favor to the customer.

terms.definition: The drop in required buyer-seller contacts when an intermediary is inserted: 5 producers selling to 20 retailers need 5 x 20 = 100 direct contacts, but routing through one wholesaler needs only 5 + 20 = 25. The M x N to M + N shift, not friendliness of service, is the economic justification for paying an intermediary a margin.
terms.whyItMatters: A distribution roleplay that asks you to defend adding a wholesaler is scored on whether you can produce the contact math; judges reject the vague answer that a middleman 'saves time.'

terms.definition: The percentage of the labor force actively seeking work but unable to find it.
terms.whyItMatters: It signals economic health and shapes consumer spending and hiring.

terms.definition: Paid, nonpersonal communication delivered through media to large audiences.
terms.whyItMatters: Advertising builds broad brand awareness efficiently and at scale.

terms.definition: Tufte's format for comparison: a grid of miniature charts sharing identical axes, identical scales and identical design, with exactly one variable changing from panel to panel - one region, one month or one product each. Holding the scale constant across every panel is the whole specification, and letting each panel auto-scale to its own data is the most common way the format is faked, because it destroys the comparison it exists to make.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-visualization task that hands you five years of sales across eight stores is scored on choosing this over one line chart with eight tangled series.

terms.definition: The opening contact and strategy used to engage a potential customer.
terms.whyItMatters: A professional approach sets the first impression that drives interest.

terms.definition: Federal rules under which gift card funds may not expire for at least 5 years from the date of the last load, and an inactivity fee may not be charged unless the card has gone unused for at least 12 months and then no more than once per month, with every fee disclosed on the card itself.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail service roleplay about a card the customer says has expired turns on whether the balance is still owed, and the numbers are the answer.

terms.definition: Creating clear, unbiased questions that collect reliable data.
terms.whyItMatters: Good design yields valid data; poor design introduces error.

terms.definition: The overall approach a business uses to reach customers and meet marketing goals.
terms.whyItMatters: Case studies require strategies that fit business objectives and market conditions.

terms.definition: The benefit a customer believes they receive compared with the cost or effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Value helps explain why a customer chooses one offer over another.

terms.definition: The empirical rule that each percentage point of unemployment above the natural rate costs roughly 2% of potential real GDP, so an economy running 3 points above that rate is producing about 6% less than its capacity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give an actual unemployment rate and a natural rate and ask what output is being lost are solved with this two-to-one ratio rather than by describing the recession in words.

terms.definition: One percent of all the households or people in a market's universe, counted whether or not their set is switched on, so a program watched by 90,000 homes in a 1,500,000-household market rates 6.0.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-per-point math on the marketing exam starts here, and competitors lose the item by treating the figure as a share of viewers rather than a percent of the whole market.

terms.definition: The highest-ranking class of motion in Robert's Rules - adjourn, recess, raise a question of privilege, call for the orders of the day - urgent enough that it may be made while other business is pending and outranks every subsidiary motion. Because it does not relate to the pending question it is undebatable in most forms, and its rank is exactly why a motion to adjourn can be made while an amendment is on the floor but an amendment cannot be made while adjournment is.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that ask which motion may be made while another is still pending are testing the precedence ladder, and this class is its top rung.

terms.definition: The buyer's tendency to judge a price against the first figure they encounter, so a $199 compare-at number makes $149 read as a bargain. Marketers separate the internal reference price a shopper carries in memory from the external one printed on the tag, and the FTC requires that any advertised former price actually have been charged.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotional-pricing roleplays ask a candidate to defend a compare-at price to a judge, which needs both the psychology and the former-price disclosure rule.

terms.definition: Number of open opportunities multiplied by average deal size multiplied by win rate, all divided by the average sales cycle length in days, which yields revenue per day: 50 x $4,000 x 0.30 / 60 days = $1,000 a day. It is the one common metric where shortening the cycle raises revenue without adding a single new prospect.
terms.whyItMatters: When an exam item asks which of four fixes lifts revenue fastest, the velocity formula shows that cutting cycle time is a divisor change and beats a small win-rate gain.

terms.definition: Support organized around closing each contact quickly and cheaply, measured on handle time and cost per contact, with no expectation the same employee ever sees that customer again. A relationship model assigns named ownership and is measured on lifetime value and retention, accepting longer contacts to win a larger share of future spend — the two sets of targets contradict each other if mixed.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the model is the first decision in a customer-strategy roleplay, because every metric the competitor then proposes has to follow from it.

terms.definition: The ceiling on category demand in a defined area and period — every possible buyer times the maximum quantity each could buy times unit price; one firm's share of that ceiling is sales potential, and the volume it actually expects to sell on the funded budget is the sales forecast.
terms.whyItMatters: Sizing items on the marketing exam hand you a population, a purchase rate and a price and expect the whole-industry ceiling, not one company's number; in a market-identification roleplay the judge is listening for the three-step narrowing said in order.

terms.definition: Assigns every small geographic unit — a ZIP+4 or a census block group of roughly 100 to 200 households — to a lifestyle cluster by joining census demographics to purchase data, on the assumption that neighbors buy alike; Nielsen's PRIZM sorts U.S. neighborhoods into 68 such clusters, so media and direct mail are bought against a cluster code rather than against an age band.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and direct-mail roleplays reward naming the cluster system and the unit it works at; saying 'we will target that ZIP code' without the cluster logic reads as guessing.

terms.definition: The labor force — everyone employed or actively searching within the last four weeks — divided by the civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over, times 100. It can fall at the same time as the unemployment rate, because a discouraged worker who stops searching leaves the numerator and the jobless count simultaneously.
terms.whyItMatters: Items pair a falling unemployment rate with a falling participation rate and ask whether the labor market really improved; the arithmetic of who leaves the labor force is what settles it.

terms.definition: Defect count divided by units shipped, times 1,000,000: 35 rejects out of 500,000 units is 70, the scale supplier scorecards use because the same figure written as a percentage -- 0.007% -- rounds toward nothing and cannot separate a good supplier from an excellent one.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays hand you competing quality records; comparing them on this scale, rather than on a rounded percentage, is what makes the recommendation defensible.

terms.definition: Short-term incentives like coupons, contests, and discounts that spur purchases.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotions drive quick sales, trial, and inventory clearance.

terms.definition: A written instruction, issued the moment a company reasonably anticipates a dispute, that suspends every routine deletion schedule and directs named custodians to preserve emails, chat threads, drafts and text messages on the subject. The duty attaches before any complaint is filed, and letting an auto-delete rule keep running past that point is what converts ordinary records management into spoliation, exposing the company to an adverse-inference instruction at trial.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-risk items that ask what an employee must do with a group chat once a customer threatens to sue are testing this duty and, above all, its trigger point.

terms.definition: Asking questions to understand a customer's problems, goals, and requirements.
terms.whyItMatters: Assessing needs ensures recommendations truly solve the customer's problem.

terms.definition: The merchant's rebuttal after a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank — compelling evidence such as delivery confirmation and the authorization record is filed inside the network's response window, commonly 30 days. Losing costs the sale plus a fee of roughly $15 to $100, and a dispute ratio approaching 1% of transactions drops the merchant into a network monitoring program.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-dispute roleplay rewards the competitor who separates a chargeback from an ordinary refund and knows the evidence deadline is not negotiable.

terms.definition: Discovering and defining the markets where a business can sell its offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Identifying the right market is the foundation of any marketing plan.

terms.definition: The International Chamber of Commerce's standard three-letter trade terms fixing exactly where risk of loss and the duty to pay carriage, insurance and customs clearance pass from seller to buyer. Under FOB risk shifts when the goods are loaded at the named port; under CIF the seller pays freight and insurance to destination yet risk still shifts at shipment; under DDP the seller carries everything, import duties included, to the buyer's door.
terms.whyItMatters: Import/export roleplays about a container damaged mid-ocean are decided entirely by which term the invoice named.

terms.definition: Sorts U.S. adults into eight consumer types on two axes — primary motivation (ideals, achievement or self-expression) and level of resources and innovation — with Innovators at the top of the resource axis and Survivors at the bottom; it classifies the individual from a survey instrument, whereas PRIZM classifies the neighborhood from census and purchase data, so the two cannot be used interchangeably.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge asks which segmentation system you would buy, naming VALS and stating its two axes shows you know the difference between a person-level and a household-level system.

terms.definition: The ability to produce a good at a lower OPPORTUNITY cost than a trading partner, which is what makes trade mutually profitable even when one country is more efficient at producing everything. Absolute advantage — simply making more per hour of input — does not by itself establish any reason to trade.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade items give a two-country, two-good output table and ask who should specialize in what; the answer comes from the opportunity-cost ratios, not from whichever column of raw output is larger.

terms.definition: The percentage of sets actually in use that are tuned to a given program, so a show rating 6 in a market where only half the sets are on carries a 12 — the figure is always larger than the program's own rating because its denominator is smaller.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a rating and this figure for the same program and ask which one a national advertiser should buy against; the answer is the rating, because only it is measured against the full market a campaign is paying to cover.

terms.definition: The measured luminance relationship between text and the background behind it under the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, expressed from 1:1 to 21:1. Level AA requires at least 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text - 18 point, or 14 point bold - plus 3:1 for interface components and meaningful graphics; level AAA raises body text to 7:1. Light grey captions and a pale brand colour on a white slide are the two failures that show up most.
terms.whyItMatters: A written event or presentation judged on accessibility is scored on naming the threshold your deck actually meets, not on asserting that the colours look readable.

terms.definition: Units of a specific add-on sold divided by units of the primary product sold, times 100 — 300 protection plans on 1,000 phones is 30%. It scores one named pairing, where cross-sell measurement counts every additional category a customer buys, so a store can raise total cross-sell revenue while this figure falls.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays that set an accessories goal are graded on whether you name the ratio you will move and the counter behavior that moves it, not on a general promise to sell more.

terms.definition: Letting one strong impression, often a single outstanding trait, lift every unrelated rating for the same person; its inverse, the horns effect, drags them all down from one bad impression. In an appraisal it shows up as suspiciously uniform scores across dimensions that ought to vary, and the standard counter is rating every employee on one dimension at a time before moving to the next.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows an evaluation form with identical scores in every category is testing this, and an HR roleplay on fixing a review process is scored on the dimension-by-dimension fix.

terms.definition: Any gap between what the customer expected and what was delivered, including delivery that met every internal specification — a technically perfect order arriving after a promised time has failed. A defect is a measurable breach of a standard the company set, so every defect is a failure while many failures pass every internal check, which is why complaint data can never be replaced by quality-control data.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the operation insists nothing went wrong is won by naming this distinction before proposing the remedy.

terms.definition: One company's maximum obtainable slice of category demand — market potential multiplied by the highest share it could hold with unlimited marketing effort; it always sits above the sales forecast, which discounts that ceiling down to the effort and budget actually approved.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that give an industry ceiling and a best-case share expect this middle figure, and a competitor who reports it as the forecast overstates the plan's revenue line in front of a judge.

terms.definition: The way customers decide what, when, where, and why to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding buying-behavior factors lets competitors target the right message and offer.

terms.definition: The total market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a year.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP is the standard gauge of economic health competitors reference.

terms.definition: Direct, person-to-person communication to inform, persuade, and build relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: It enables customized pitches and problem-solving for high-value sales.

terms.definition: An institution such as a bank, credit union, or brokerage that offers money-management products.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right provider is a recurring judgment in personal-finance scenarios.

terms.definition: Giving full attention, checking understanding, and responding thoughtfully to a speaker.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect competitors to handle questions and concerns clearly.

terms.definition: A product's characteristics and the value those characteristics give.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must separate features from benefits to sell effectively.

terms.definition: A privacy demand the business must first authenticate as coming from the consumer, then answer within 45 days, extendable once by a further 45 with notice, covering the categories collected in the preceding 12 months. It must be handled free of charge unless it is manifestly unfounded or excessive, and acting on it without verifying identity is itself a breach.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a caller demands their records deleted tests whether the competitor verifies identity before acting and can state the response clock.

terms.definition: Sizing demand from the bottom up: identify every potential buyer in each segment or territory, estimate units each would buy, and sum units times price across them. The chain-ratio method runs the opposite direction, starting from a national total and multiplying it down through successive percentages.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business sizing cases on the exam name a count of establishments and a per-establishment purchase rate, which is a buildup problem; using a national percentage chain there produces the wrong answer.

terms.definition: A candidate group qualifies as a market segment only if it passes five named tests — measurable (its size and buying power can be quantified), substantial (large and profitable enough to serve alone), accessible (reachable through some channel or medium), differentiable (it responds differently from other segments to a change in the mix) and actionable (the firm can actually build and run a program for it); failing any one of the five makes it a description of people, not a segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Market-planning roleplays that ask you to defend a chosen segment are scored on running it against the criteria out loud; the segment competitors usually pick fails 'substantial' or 'accessible'.

terms.definition: An appraisal method that requires managers to sort employees into fixed proportions — often 20% top, 70% middle and 10% bottom — regardless of how the group actually performed, so a strong team must still produce a bottom 10%. Its counterpart, a behaviorally anchored rating scale, rates each person against written behavior standards with no quota, which is why the two produce different outcomes for the same identical team.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect the quota objection when a roleplay asks whether to adopt ranking: rating a high-performing department this way forces an unfair low rating.

terms.definition: The complete record of a nation's transactions with the rest of the world — the current account of goods, services, income and transfers, plus the capital and financial accounts — which sums to zero by construction, since a current-account deficit is financed by an offsetting inflow of capital. The balance of trade is only the goods-and-services slice of the current account.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items ask what a persistent trade deficit implies; the correct answer follows the offsetting capital inflow rather than treating the deficit as unfunded loss.

terms.definition: The number of exposures needed inside a single purchase cycle before a message registers at all — below it the spend is wasted and above it the spend is redundant. The working planning standard is three exposures, from Krugman's three-hit theory.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client wants the budget spread over more vehicles is a test of this: adding vehicles raises reach but can drop everyone below three exposures, leaving a campaign that technically touched the market and communicated nothing.

terms.definition: A readability score that converts a passage into a U.S. school grade: 0.39 x (total words / total sentences) + 11.8 x (total syllables / total words) - 15.59. Because sentence length is multiplied by 0.39 and syllable count by 11.8, swapping 'utilize' for 'use' moves the score less than splitting one 30-word sentence into two 15-word ones; consumer-facing documents are normally targeted at grade 8 or below.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to rewrite a return policy for shoppers is scored on whether you can name a measurable target and the two levers that hit it, instead of promising to 'make it simpler.'

terms.definition: A six-part qualification framework — Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion — that adds the buyer's internal mechanics, the written criteria and the approval path, to the money-and-authority checks BANT stops at. It is built for long committee purchases where the signer is never the first contact.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business roleplay with a committee, naming the economic buyer and the decision criteria is the specific step judges look for before any presentation content.

terms.definition: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's implementing rule, a consumer has 60 days from the statement showing a disputed debit-card or ACH transfer to notify the bank; the bank then has 10 business days to investigate, or may extend to 45 calendar days only if it posts provisional credit inside those 10 days, and must report its findings within 3 business days of finishing. Liability for a lost card is capped at $50 when reported within 2 business days of discovery and $500 after that. Credit-card charges are excluded — those run on the Fair Credit Billing Act's two-billing-cycle track.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services or banking roleplay in which a client's debit card was drained overnight is scored on whether the competitor cites the 10-business-day investigation and the provisional-credit condition, instead of promising an immediate refund no associate can authorize.

terms.definition: A descriptive attribute that changes over time and forces a documented choice: Type 1 overwrites the old value and loses all history, while Type 2 closes the existing row with an end date and inserts a new version row, so a sale made two years ago still ties to the sales territory that was in force on the day it happened.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge asks why last year's totals shifted after a store was reassigned to a new district, the answer is which of these two handling types the warehouse used.

terms.definition: The specific customer group a business chooses as its primary marketing audience.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommendations are stronger when they name a specific audience.

terms.definition: The blend of product, price, place, and promotion used to reach a target market.
terms.whyItMatters: The four Ps are the standard framework for building a marketing recommendation.

terms.definition: The theory that exchange rates should adjust until an identical basket of goods costs the same in both countries: if a burger is $5 in the U.S. and £4 in Britain, the implied rate is $1.25 per pound, and a market rate of $1.60 says the pound is overvalued. Trade barriers and non-traded services keep real rates from converging to it.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items give two local prices for one product and ask what the exchange rate implies, or ask why a salary converts to very different living standards in two countries.

terms.definition: Activities that build positive relationships with the public and media.
terms.whyItMatters: PR manages image, trust, and credibility through third-party voices.

terms.definition: A letter layout in which every element - date, inside address, salutation, body, complimentary close and signature block - begins flush at the left margin with no indentation, set on one-inch margins with a blank line between parts and no blank-line indents inside paragraphs. Modified block, its near neighbour, moves the date and the closing to start at the horizontal center of the page; semi-block does that and also indents the first line of each paragraph.
terms.whyItMatters: Formatting items on the exam give you the same letter three ways and ask which is full block, and written-event submissions lose presentation points for mixing two of the three.

terms.definition: A deliverable-oriented decomposition of a project into progressively smaller work packages governed by the 100 percent rule — the children of any element must sum to exactly that element, no more and no less — so it captures scope, not sequence, which the schedule adds afterward.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how to start planning a project, the accepted first move is decomposing deliverables before estimating or scheduling, and the completeness rule is what stops forgotten work becoming a budget overrun.

terms.definition: A method built on teach, tailor and take control, in which the rep opens with a commercial insight that reframes how the buyer sees their own business and then respectfully pushes back on the buyer's assumptions. Relationship selling does the reverse: it builds trust first and delivers whatever the buyer already says they want.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay judged on demonstrating expertise rewards teaching the buyer something about their own market, while a purely agreeable rep reads as an order taker.

terms.definition: Links internal service quality to employee satisfaction and retention, then to productivity and delivered value, then to customer loyalty and finally revenue growth. The practical claim is that the cheapest lever on the customer end of the chain usually sits at the employee end, so a loyalty problem is often a scheduling or training problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Backs a roleplay recommendation to fix rostering or training when the case presents falling guest satisfaction as the problem.

terms.definition: The smoothed yearly rate that carries a starting value to an ending value over n years: (ending value / beginning value)^(1/n) - 1. It deliberately hides year-to-year swings, so a category that jumped 40% and then fell 20% still reports one steady rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan questions that give a market size for two years and a span expect this exponent, not the two values subtracted and divided by the number of years.

terms.definition: Empirical pattern in which roughly the top 20% of a category's buyers generate about 80% of its volume, and the heavier half of buyers accounts for 80% to 90% of units in many packaged-goods categories — so a 10% lift among heavy users is worth several times the same percentage lift among light users, and a promotion measured in customers reached can be worth less than one measured in volume reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-budget roleplays that ask where to spend a limited fund are won by weighting the target by consumption share rather than by headcount.

terms.definition: The value of mutually beneficial trades destroyed when price is pushed away from the market-clearing level by a tax, a ceiling, a floor or a monopoly. On a supply-and-demand diagram it is the triangle between the two curves over the lost quantity — one-half base times height — and it goes to no one: not the buyer, not the seller, not the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask who bears the cost of a per-unit tax and answer with the split of the burden plus this un-captured loss; naming only the tax revenue is an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: An orderly, methodical approach to tasks and decisions that follows a logical structure.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges favor structured reasoning over a scattered approach.

terms.definition: The share of the target exposed at or above the threshold number of times — conventionally three or more — so a schedule with 70% total reach may deliver only 35% of this, because the half of the audience that saw the ad once or twice does not count toward it.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-plan items give a reach curve and a frequency distribution and ask which of two schedules performs better; the one with lower total reach usually wins because more of its audience cleared the three-exposure threshold.

terms.definition: A formal written message with a clear subject, correct grammar, and appropriate tone.
terms.whyItMatters: Written events reward mastery of email conventions.

terms.definition: Connecting a product feature to the benefit the customer receives.
terms.whyItMatters: It turns product facts into customer value.

terms.term: Fair Credit Billing Act billing-error window
terms.definition: A credit-card holder must dispute a charge in writing within 60 days of the statement date on which it first appeared; the issuer then has 30 days to acknowledge the notice and two complete billing cycles — never more than 90 days — to resolve it, and may not report the disputed amount as delinquent while the claim is open. It reaches open-end credit only, so the same $400 charge disputed on a debit card is handled instead under Regulation E's 10-business-day investigation.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law and finance exam items pair this window against the debit-card rule, and a customer-complaint roleplay about a double-billed credit-card charge expects the competitor to state the 60-day filing deadline before offering any goodwill.

terms.definition: A written document laying out marketing objectives, strategies, and tactics for a period.
terms.whyItMatters: The plan guides all promotional and customer-facing decisions.

terms.definition: Cost savings that come from producing several different products with shared inputs, so total cost of making A and B together is below the cost of two separate firms making them; economies of scale instead lower the per-unit cost of one product as its own volume rises.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a bakery adding catering with the same ovens and staff and ask which cost advantage applies, where 'scale' is the planted wrong answer.

terms.definition: One brand's sales to a single customer divided by that customer's total category spending over the same period — a household that spends $400 a year on coffee and $120 of it at one chain gives that chain 30% — so it is a per-customer ratio, unlike market share, which divides a brand's sales by the whole category's sales across all buyers; a brand can hold flat market share while its wallet share collapses.
terms.whyItMatters: Customer-relations roleplays that ask how to grow revenue without new customers are answered with this ratio and the cross-sell that raises it.

terms.definition: The principle that adding more of one input eventually yields less added output.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why scaling operations becomes less efficient past a point.

terms.definition: Unpaid media coverage generated through PR, news, and referrals.
terms.whyItMatters: Publicity builds credibility through sources other than paid ads.

terms.definition: An arrangement that puts the main idea, request or answer in the very first sentence and places explanation after it - correct for routine requests, good news, and most internal messages, and expected by busy or senior readers. The indirect pattern reverses that into four ordered parts: a neutral buffer, the reasons, the bad news itself stated once, and a goodwill close. Choose by predicted reaction, not by topic: a refusal a reader already expects can still be written directly.
terms.whyItMatters: The most common written-event error is burying a recommendation in paragraph three of a message the reader will happily agree with.

terms.definition: An advance paid to a rep against commission not yet earned — a $3,000 monthly draw against $2,200 of earnings leaves $800 outstanding. A recoverable draw carries that $800 forward against next month's commissions, while a non-recoverable draw forgives it, which makes the second version a guaranteed minimum in everything but name.
terms.whyItMatters: Human-resources and selling exam items ask which pay plan protects a new rep during a long ramp, and the recoverable-versus-non-recoverable distinction is the answer's hinge.

terms.definition: Friction between firms at the SAME stage of a channel — two franchisees of one brand advertising into each other's trade area, or two dealers discounting against each other. Vertical channel conflict, by contrast, runs between DIFFERENT stages: a manufacturer and its distributor fighting over margin or over the manufacturer's own web store.
terms.whyItMatters: A channel-management roleplay hands you an angry dealer and asks for a fix; the remedy differs by type — territory rules settle horizontal disputes, margin or policy changes settle vertical ones.

terms.definition: Sessions a virtual agent closes without handing the customer to a live representative, divided by every session that virtual agent opened — a bot that finishes 700 of 1,000 chats and passes 300 along contains 70%. The denominator is bot sessions only, which is what separates it from a self-service deflection rate measured against total support demand, so a bot nobody reaches can post a high containment figure while deflecting almost nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A customer-service management roleplay that asks a competitor to justify a chatbot's return turns on this pair of denominators; quoting containment as though it were deflection overstates the labor saved and a judge listening for cost per contact will catch it.

terms.definition: The portion of total addressable demand a firm's product, price point and channels can actually reach — the total narrowed to the segments and geographies it serves. Narrow it once more by the share realistically winnable in the plan period and you have the serviceable obtainable market.
terms.whyItMatters: Written-event plans that state one giant industry figure lose points; judges expect the total narrowed twice, with the reason for each cut named.

terms.definition: A philosophy that focuses all business activities on satisfying customer needs profitably.
terms.whyItMatters: It reminds competitors that every tactic should trace back to a real customer need.

terms.definition: Passes a strict two-part test: non-excludable, meaning a non-payer cannot be kept from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is left for anyone else. National defense and a lighthouse qualify; cable television is excludable and a crowded highway is rival, so neither does — which is why private firms underprovide the real thing and taxes fund it.
terms.whyItMatters: Items list several government-provided services and ask which genuinely meets the economic definition; roads, schools and parks fail one prong each and are the intended distractors.

terms.definition: A schedule carrying a low continuous weight all year with heavier bursts layered over the peak selling weeks, so unlike flighting the brand is never entirely off air, and unlike continuity the weekly weight is not flat.
terms.whyItMatters: A client with year-round sales and a holiday spike is the standard prompt for this pattern; naming it and drawing the line against the other two schedules is what separates a scored answer from a vague one.

terms.definition: Whether an instrument truly measures the abstract idea it claims to, so a three-item loyalty battery may in fact be capturing nothing but recent convenience; this is a separate question from reliability, which only asks whether repeated administrations agree, and a broken thermometer reading 50 every single time is perfectly reliable and completely invalid.
terms.whyItMatters: Assessing whether a proposed study will actually answer the business question, this is the distinction a judge listens for when a competitor defends an instrument.

terms.definition: A five-step persuasive outline - attention, need, satisfaction, visualization, action - where the fourth step is the one that distinguishes it: the audience is walked through a vivid picture of life after adopting the proposal (or of life if they refuse) before any request is made. A plain problem-solution outline stops after satisfaction, and a call to action without the visualization step is the most common way competitors flatten it back into three parts.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks you to sell a manager on a new procedure, this sequence gives a scored structure; naming the five steps beats an unstructured pitch every time.

terms.definition: A structured pitch showing how an offering meets the customer's needs.
terms.whyItMatters: A compelling presentation moves a prospect toward purchase.

terms.definition: A concession — a discount, a credit, or a downgrade to a cheaper plan — put in front of a customer at the moment they state an intent to cancel, and priced by a margin test: the ceiling is the gross margin still expected over the account's remaining tenure minus what winning that customer back would cost, so a 30% discount on a subscription carrying a 25% gross margin destroys value even though the account is retained. It is offered before cancellation is processed, unlike a win-back campaign, which targets customers who have already gone.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that hands a competitor a cancelling account expects the concession to be defended with the account's remaining margin and acquisition cost, not with the largest discount the associate is allowed to give.

terms.definition: The slice of the serviceable available market a company expects to capture within the plan horizon: SAM times a realistic share percentage, so a $200 million SAM at 4% share is an $8 million target. Unlike SAM it is a forecast the plan is held to, not a ceiling.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the number a judge compares against the plan's revenue projection and marketing budget; a SOM larger than the funded plan can deliver is the fastest way to lose credibility in a presentation.

terms.definition: The percentage of a category's national sales occurring in one market divided by the percentage of the national population living there, multiplied by 100 — a metro holding 2% of the population but 3% of category sales scores 150 — where 100 is exactly average and anything above it means the category is over-developed in that market regardless of how any single brand performs there.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-allocation roleplays ask which markets deserve the spend; the index pair, not gut feel about city size, is what a judge expects to hear.

terms.definition: A supplier rule conditioning co-op advertising support on retailers not promoting below a stated figure, while leaving the actual transaction price untouched. Announced unilaterally under the Colgate doctrine it involves no agreement at all, which is why it carries less antitrust exposure than resale price maintenance.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-conflict roleplays about a retailer's online listing are resolved by knowing that what is controlled is the advertised number, not the price the customer pays at checkout.

terms.definition: Increased risk-taking AFTER an agreement is signed because someone else now bears the downside — an insured driver who stops locking the car, a bank lending recklessly while expecting a rescue. Adverse selection is the mirror problem BEFORE signing, when the riskiest applicants are the most eager buyers and the seller cannot tell them apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Items describing a party who behaves worse once protected are testing the before-versus-after timing that separates these two information problems; the timing is the whole answer.

terms.definition: The channels ads run on — TV, radio, print, digital, outdoor, and social.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right media reaches the target audience cost-effectively.

terms.definition: A formal document in standard format used for official outside communication.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect correct formatting, tone, and structure.

terms.definition: A higher commission rate applied only to revenue above quota — 8% up to plan and 12% beyond it — so each dollar of overperformance pays more than the first dollar did. A cap or a decelerator does the reverse and is precisely what tempts a rep to hold a signed deal until the next period opens.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on motivating a sales force ask which plan change stops sandbagging at quarter end, and the rate structure above quota is the mechanism being tested.

terms.definition: Contacts an agent passes to another agent or queue, divided by contacts that agent handled — 40 hand-offs across 500 calls is 8%. It counts lateral moves to a peer at the same authority level, whereas an escalation rate counts only contacts pushed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier, so a caller routed sideways to a billing specialist raises this figure and leaves escalation untouched. Every transfer also breaks first contact resolution, even when the second agent solves the issue on the same call.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on resolving service situations, a competitor proposing skills-based routing has to say which of the two ratios the change should move, since routing callers correctly the first time cuts transfers without touching escalations.

terms.definition: The share of units clearing a step with no rework or scrap; multiplied across steps it gives rolled throughput yield, so four stations each at 95% deliver only 0.95^4 = 81.5% clean units, meaning a line whose every station reports 95% is really losing almost one unit in five.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality roleplays are scored on catching hidden rework: each station passing its own target while the finished-goods number falls short is exactly the scenario this calculation explains.

terms.definition: An assessment of internal and external factors affecting a business's marketing.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding the situation must come before any recommendation.

terms.definition: The bundle of benefits a business promises to deliver to a specific customer group.
terms.whyItMatters: A sharp value proposition anchors positioning, messaging, and pricing.

terms.definition: Focusing on producing the goods or services in which one has a comparative advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Specialization improves efficiency and is the basis of trade.

terms.definition: Media cost divided by impressions delivered and multiplied by 1,000 — a $6,000 magazine page reaching 400,000 readers is $15 — the conversion that makes a cheap small vehicle and an expensive large one directly comparable.
