terms.whyItMatters: The most common media-math item on the marketing exam gives two vehicles with different prices and different audiences and asks which is the better buy; the raw price answers nothing and this figure answers it in one step.

terms.definition: An argument broken into six named parts: the claim, the grounds (the data offered), the warrant - the usually unstated assumption that licenses moving from the grounds to the claim - plus backing that supports the warrant, a qualifier that limits how strongly the claim holds, and a rebuttal that names the conditions under which it fails. Arguments collapse at the warrant far more often than at the data, because the missing piece was never said aloud.
terms.whyItMatters: Defending a recommendation to a judge who pushes back means naming the assumption connecting your figures to your conclusion, which is the step competitors skip when they simply repeat the data louder.

terms.definition: Two distinct prohibitions in one statute: an anti-bribery provision barring the offer or payment of anything of value to a foreign official to obtain or retain business, and a books-and-records provision requiring issuers to keep accurate accounts and adequate internal accounting controls, which is how most cases are actually charged. Narrow carve-outs cover small facilitating payments for routine non-discretionary acts and payments expressly lawful under the host country's written law.
terms.whyItMatters: International-expansion roleplays ask whether a fee paid to speed a routine permit is legal, and the facilitating-payment carve-out decides it.

terms.definition: Responding to a customer's concerns in a helpful, persuasive way.
terms.whyItMatters: Handling objections improves trust and conversion.

terms.definition: Section 102(c) of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act forbids conditioning a written warranty on the buyer's use of a branded part or an authorized service center unless the warrantor supplies that part or service free of charge or holds an FTC waiver — so an independent repair shop cannot by itself void coverage, and neither can failing to mail back a registration card, because the purchase date is what proves the claim. A service contract sold for separate consideration is not a warranty and never falls under this rule.
terms.whyItMatters: An automotive- or electronics-services roleplay where a guest was told their warranty died because they used an outside mechanic is scored on interpreting the policy correctly to the customer rather than repeating the store's line.

terms.definition: One percentage point of category share, worth 1% of total industry sales in dollars — $40 million in a $4 billion category. Moving from 10% to 11% share is one point but an 11% relative gain, and plans state objectives in points precisely to keep the two apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Objective-setting items ask what a stated share gain is worth in revenue, which requires multiplying the point value by industry sales rather than by the company's own sales.

terms.definition: The percentage of one brand's national sales made in a market divided by that market's percentage of national population, times 100; read against the category index it sorts markets into four actions — high BDI with low CDI means a strong brand in a weak category, while low BDI with high CDI is the classic opportunity market where the category sells well and the brand does not, and both indexes below 100 argues for withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: The paired index read is the standard answer to a roleplay asking which market to defend and which to invest in; giving one index without the other gets a follow-up you cannot answer.

terms.definition: Divide 70 by an annual growth rate written in whole percentage points to get the years a quantity needs to double: real output growing 3.5% a year doubles in 20 years, while 7% growth doubles it in 10 — so a one-point difference in growth is a decade of living standards.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade and economic-development items ask which of two developing markets a firm should enter first; the answer turns on doubling time, not on this year's growth number.

terms.definition: Deci and Ryan's account of motivation as three psychological needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — plus a continuum running from purely external regulation through introjected and identified regulation to fully internalized motivation. Motivation is therefore a location on that continuum rather than an amount, and only the internalized end keeps working once the supervisor stops watching.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking why a bonus program stopped producing results, or a roleplay on motivating a team without extra budget, is scored on giving choice, competence feedback and belonging instead of raising the payout.

terms.definition: What one rating point of a market costs: spot price divided by the program's rating, so a $3,000 spot on a 5-rated program is $600. It prices a percentage of a market where cost per thousand prices raw impressions, which is why it cannot be compared across markets of different sizes.
terms.whyItMatters: Broadcast-buying items ask a competitor to rank stations within one market, where this is the right measure, then ask to compare a small market against a large one, where it is the wrong one and cost per thousand is needed instead.

terms.definition: Tufte's distortion metric: the size of the effect shown in the graphic divided by the size of the effect in the data, where an honest chart lands between 0.95 and 1.05. A 20 percent rise drawn as a bar twice as tall scores 5; scaling a pictogram by both height and width doubles a doubling into a fourfold area, scoring about 2. A truncated vertical axis inflates it the same way, which is why a bar chart's axis must start at zero even when a line chart's need not.
terms.whyItMatters: Data-visualization items give a chart and ask why it misleads, and the scored answer names the exaggeration, not just 'the graph looks unfair.'

terms.definition: Sizing territories by the work each contains: accounts multiplied by the calls per year each requires, divided by the calls one rep can make — 400 accounts needing 12 calls each is 4,800 calls, and at 800 calls per rep that is six territories. The breakdown method instead divides a sales forecast by average revenue per rep and ignores how much service each account demands.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay asking you to rebalance territories after a merger wants the calculation and the service load, not an even split of the map.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.definition: The share of industry unit volume a plan must win just to cover its fixed costs: fixed costs / contribution margin per unit gives break-even units, then those units / total industry units. $2,000,000 of fixed cost at $10 contribution needs 200,000 units, which is 5% of a 4-million-unit category.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product plans are judged on whether the required share is plausible against the shares incumbents already hold; a break-even share above the category leader's is a plan a judge will reject on sight.

terms.definition: Balances owed divided by total available revolving credit, weighted heavily in a credit score and generally kept under 30% to avoid a penalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Credit-score advising roleplays reward the competitor who tells a client to pay down balances or raise a limit instead of closing an unused card.

terms.definition: Distinct customers who bought at least once in a period divided by the total defined target population, as a percentage — 40,000 buyers out of a 500,000-person target is 8% — which counts buyers, not units or dollars; that is exactly what separates it from market share, so a brand can raise share by selling more to the same people while its penetration does not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Growth roleplays hinge on whether the plan should recruit new buyers or sell more to current ones, and this is the number that tells the judge you know which lever you chose.

terms.definition: Actual real GDP minus potential real GDP, divided by potential and multiplied by 100. Actual output of $19.4 trillion against potential of $20 trillion is a gap of −3%, the recessionary case that pulls prices and hiring down; a positive gap signals an overheating economy.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle questions give an actual and a potential output figure and expect the sign and the percentage, not the word 'slowdown'.

terms.definition: Targeted messages sent straight to individuals by mail, email, or phone.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct marketing allows personalized, measurable, one-to-one engagement.

terms.definition: Interference produced by the message's own words - unfamiliar jargon, an ambiguous pronoun, a term whose connotation differs for sender and receiver - as opposed to physical noise, which is external to the message (a loud room, a dropped call, small type), and psychological noise, which is inside the receiver (anxiety, distraction, a prior grudge). The distinction decides the fix: repeating the sentence louder cures only the physical kind.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam scenario where a customer misreads a policy term is a semantic-noise item, and the scored remedy is rewording, not resending.

terms.definition: Asking for the order or finalizing the agreement to complete the sale.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing when and how to close prevents lost opportunities.

terms.definition: Sets the conditions under which a worker 40 or older can validly waive an age claim in exchange for severance: at least 21 days to consider the agreement, a 7-day period to revoke after signing, written advice to consult an attorney, and consideration beyond what was already owed. In a group layoff the consideration period stretches to 45 days and the employer must disclose the job titles and ages of everyone selected and everyone spared.
terms.whyItMatters: Drafting a severance offer in a downsizing roleplay is incomplete without the review and revocation periods, and the group-layoff disclosure is the detail judges reward.

terms.definition: The total profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: CLV guides how much to invest in retention and service.

terms.definition: A review of a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
terms.whyItMatters: SWOT gives a structured frame for the situation analysis behind a plan.

terms.definition: The core marketing activities such as pricing, promotion, selling, and distribution.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors organize their analysis around which marketing functions a decision touches.

terms.definition: Money stock times the number of times each dollar is spent equals the price level times real output: M × V = P × Q. Restated in growth rates, %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔQ, so with turnover steady and output rising 2%, an 8% jump in the money stock leaves about 6% inflation.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate and inflation items ask what happens to prices when the central bank expands the money stock faster than the economy grows; this identity produces the number.

terms.definition: Total media spend divided by completed conversions rather than by clicks — $800 producing 16 purchases is $50, even though that same $800 buying 3,200 clicks made cost per click look like $0.25. Rising here with a flat cost per click means the landing page, not the media, is failing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item showing cheap clicks and expensive customers is testing whether the competitor can locate the failure downstream of the ad, and a roleplay client who wants to cut the ad budget is usually the one who needs the page fixed.

terms.definition: The person accountable for the day-to-day quality, field definitions and correction of one data domain, executing rules that somebody else sets; the data owner is the business executive who sets those rules, signs off on the definitions and approves who may see the domain — accountability for the policy versus accountability for the practice.
terms.whyItMatters: Records-monitoring roleplays ask who should approve a new customer field and who should fix the 400 records already entered wrong, and the two answers are different roles.

terms.definition: Visual tools such as charts and diagrams that reinforce a message.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must select and justify aids that support their analysis.

terms.definition: The Federal Trade Commission provision giving a buyer until midnight of the third business day to cancel a sale of $25 or more made at their home or anywhere other than the seller's permanent place of business, with the seller required to hand over two dated cancellation forms at signing. Sales made inside the seller's own store are not covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal and ethical selling items on the exam test the dollar threshold and the location condition, and in-home roleplays expect you to disclose the cancellation right rather than hurry the signature.

terms.definition: A relationship of mutual understanding and trust between a business and its customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Building rapport raises trust and the odds of repeat business.

terms.definition: A weighted score for ranking candidate countries or segments: each factor gets a weight, the weights sum to 1.0, each market gets a rating, and weight times rating summed gives one comparable number — so a market that scores well on a 0.10 factor still loses to one that scores well on a 0.40 factor.
terms.whyItMatters: Expansion cases hand over a table of markets and ask which to enter first; the defensible answer weights the criteria before scoring rather than counting how many boxes each market ticks.

terms.definition: The top rung of the three-stage loyalty ladder: at recognition the buyer merely knows the mark, at preference the buyer chooses it but accepts a substitute when it is out of stock, and at insistence the buyer will leave the store or delay the purchase rather than take another brand — the only stage that lets a firm hold price through a competitor's promotion.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask what a strong brand is actually worth; naming the three stages and the out-of-stock behavior that separates preference from insistence is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Latest allowable start minus earliest possible start for a task — the delay it can absorb before the project finish moves; total float is shared along a chain, whereas free float is the smaller amount that delays no immediately following task at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a network with early and late start dates, exam questions ask how long a task can slip; confusing the shared allowance with the task-level one over-promises the client in a status roleplay.

terms.definition: The extra satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit, which declines as consumption rises — the second slice of pizza is worth less than the first. A consumer maximizes total satisfaction by spreading a budget until satisfaction per dollar is equal across goods: the marginal utility of A over the price of A equals the marginal utility of B over the price of B.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending items give utility figures and prices for two products and ask which the buyer purchases next; the per-dollar rule, not the raw utility number, decides it.

terms.definition: Customer recommendations and referrals that spread opinions about a product.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth builds organic advocacy and trust beyond paid ads.

terms.definition: Edward Hall's study of how people use physical distance, mapped to four zones: intimate from contact to about 18 inches, personal from 18 inches to 4 feet, social from 4 to 12 feet, and public beyond 12 feet. Normal business is transacted in the social zone, so a salesperson who closes to 3 feet has entered personal space and is read as pressure rather than warmth. The distances themselves are cultural, and the same 3 feet reads as ordinary in much of Latin America and as intrusive in northern Europe.
terms.whyItMatters: Nonverbal-cue items describe a customer stepping back during a demonstration, and the scored answer names the zone violation instead of calling it 'being uncomfortable.'

terms.definition: Recommending additional products based on the customer's current purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Suggestive selling raises transaction value and meets more needs.

terms.definition: Contacts fully resolved on the first interaction divided by total contacts handled — 1,200 of 1,500 is 80%. A case that is transferred to a second agent or reopened later counts as a failure even if it is solved the same day, which is why it moves in the opposite direction from average handle time whenever agents rush callers off the line.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on service improvement, the fix a competitor proposes has to raise this number; trimming call length by promising a callback lowers it.

terms.definition: Standard measure of non-degree instruction in which one unit equals 10 contact hours of participation in an accredited program, so a two-day 16-hour seminar earns 1.6 units. A college credit hour is a different currency entirely — roughly 15 contact hours across a semester — and licensing boards rarely convert one into the other.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked on the exam to price a training plan against a 40-hour renewal requirement, a competitor has to convert seminar hours into units before the budget makes sense.

terms.definition: Dividing a market into distinct groups of customers with similar needs.
terms.whyItMatters: Segmentation lets a business target specific customer groups effectively.

terms.definition: The added value a strong, well-known brand name gives a product.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand equity explains why customers pay more for, and stay loyal to, established brands.

terms.definition: −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC): with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8 it is −4, one unit smaller in size than the 5 attached to direct spending and opposite in sign, because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved rather than spent. A $100 million tax cut therefore adds about $400 million to output, not $500 million.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-and-business items ask which stimulates output more per dollar, a tax cut or direct purchases; the sign and the one-unit gap are the whole answer.

terms.definition: Revenue attributable to a campaign divided by what that campaign cost: $40,000 of revenue on $10,000 of spend is 4.0. It differs from return on investment, which subtracts cost of goods and the spend itself before dividing, so a 4.0 here is still a losing campaign at a 20% gross margin.
terms.whyItMatters: A client presenting a campaign as a four-to-one success is the setup for this distinction; the competitor is expected to ask for the margin before agreeing the campaign made money.

terms.definition: Albert Mehrabian's finding that when a speaker's words, tone and facial expression contradict each other about how they feel, listeners resolve the conflict by weighting words 7 percent, tone of voice 38 percent, and facial expression 55 percent. The routine misuse is the claim that 93 percent of all communication is nonverbal: the studies tested single words about liking, said by women, in a laboratory, and say nothing about the content of an informational message. Cited correctly, it covers incongruence only.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the standard trap answer on nonverbal-communication items, and a judge who has heard the '93 percent' line all day notices the competitor who states its actual scope.

terms.definition: Fayol's principle that each employee takes orders from exactly one supervisor, so conflicting instructions and divided accountability cannot arise; a matrix structure knowingly breaks this principle, which is why it needs a written rule for resolving competing demands.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about an employee getting contradictory priorities from two managers are scored on naming the violated principle and installing a tie-breaking rule.

terms.definition: Exaggerated subjective praise no reasonable buyer would treat as fact — the finest coffee in town — which creates no liability, as opposed to a misrepresentation, a specific factual claim about performance, condition or origin that does. The dividing test is whether the statement could be proven false.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethical selling roleplays plant a tempting overstatement, and knowing that this machine will cut your costs in half is a checkable claim while our machines are the best is not keeps you on the right side of the rubric.

terms.definition: Talk time plus hold time plus after-call work, divided by contacts handled — 6 minutes of talk, 1 minute of hold and 3 minutes of wrap-up across 40 calls averages 10 minutes. Leaving wrap-up out of the numerator is the standard error, and it makes every staffing model built on the figure understaff the queue.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing math in a peak-demand hospitality or call-center roleplay starts here, and exam items expect the wrap-up term to be inside the average.

terms.definition: (area population x annual category spending per person) / total retail selling space devoted to that category — dollars of demand per square foot of supply. A high result means demand outruns the space serving it and the trade area can carry another store; a low one means the area is already saturated.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail expansion cases hand over population, per-person spending and competitors' square footage, and the expected recommendation follows from computing this ratio rather than counting rival stores.

terms.definition: Attributes a brand must match well enough for buyers to accept it as a legitimate member of the category — a car that is safe, a bank that clears deposits — which buy entry and win no preference at all; the attributes that win preference are points of difference, and because parity is a threshold rather than a scale, money spent beating a rival on a parity attribute returns nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking where to invest a product-improvement budget is a parity-versus-difference question; spending to over-deliver on a category minimum is the error the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: A distribution path where one or more intermediaries sit between producer and customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Indirect channels widen reach and share costs but reduce producer control.

terms.definition: An ad's key elements — headline, copy, visuals, call to action, and branding.
terms.whyItMatters: Each component ensures the ad communicates its message persuasively.

terms.definition: Presenting numbers and trends visually so patterns are clear.
terms.whyItMatters: Visuals make recommendations look credible and actionable.

terms.definition: A seller's factual affirmation, description, sample or model that becomes part of the basis of the bargain, created by the statement itself with no formal words and no intent required — where an implied warranty arises automatically from the sale by operation of law. A rep quoting a performance figure in a presentation can create one without meaning to.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling exam items ask which of four salesperson statements creates a binding promise, and the answer is always the specific, checkable one rather than the general praise beside it.

terms.definition: A mindset committed to meeting customer needs and providing quality help.
terms.whyItMatters: It helps employees deliver consistent, customer-focused interactions.

terms.definition: Forecast accuracy scored as the average of |actual minus forecast| / actual across periods — a +10% miss and a -10% miss do not cancel, because the absolute value is taken before averaging. That is exactly what separates it from forecast bias, which keeps the signs.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-forecasting items give several months of forecast and actual pairs and ask how accurate the method was; averaging the signed errors returns a flattering near-zero that the item is designed to catch.

terms.definition: A standardized study a research firm runs on its own initiative and then sells to every subscriber in the category, splitting the cost across all of them; proprietary or custom research is commissioned by a single client, answers that client's exact question and stays confidential, so the trade is comparability and low price against fit and exclusivity.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommending where a small business should get category data on a tight budget, the scored distinction is why cheap shared data cannot answer a company-specific question.

terms.definition: Attributes buyers strongly associate with one brand, rate favorably, and believe no competitor delivers as well — all three conditions, not just the first — which is what makes them the reason to choose it, unlike points of parity, which only qualify the brand for the consideration set; once rivals match a claimed difference it has quietly become a parity attribute and stops moving share even though the advertising still runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to identify what sets a company apart, a competitor who names a feature every rival also offers has named a parity attribute and will be corrected on the spot.

terms.definition: One minus the share of each additional dollar of income that gets spent, so an MPC of 0.75 leaves 0.25. It is the multiplier's denominator: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, meaning the more households save out of a raise, the smaller the ripple from any injection of spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending questions give a change in income and a change in saving and expect the multiplier that follows, not a definition of thrift.

terms.definition: An auction in which the winner pays one increment above the runner-up's bid rather than the amount they themselves bid, so a $4.00 bid beating a $2.50 bid clears at $2.51 — which is why bidding true value can never cost more than that value is worth.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-buying items ask why an advertiser should enter its real maximum instead of shading the bid down; the mechanic, not the strategy, is the answer, and competitors who guess pay-what-you-bid get it backwards.

terms.definition: The nonverbal channel of body motion - posture, gesture, facial expression and eye behavior - which is distinct from paralanguage, the vocal qualities wrapped around the words (pitch, rate, volume, pauses, filled hesitations like 'um'), and from chronemics, the messages carried by the use of time such as arriving late, answering after three days, or scheduling only 10 minutes. Naming the right channel matters because each has a different repair.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that ask you to read a supervisor's crossed arms, clipped tone and delayed reply are testing three separate channels in one scenario.

terms.definition: Developing a base of regular customers who return to buy again.
terms.whyItMatters: A strong clientele provides stable revenue and drives growth.

terms.definition: The 1936 amendment to the Clayton Act barring a seller from charging competing buyers different prices for commodities of like grade and quality where competition may be injured. Two defenses exist - cost justification and meeting a competitor's price in good faith - and because it reaches goods rather than services, a service firm's tiered rates fall outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: Wholesale roleplays ask whether a special volume deal for one chain is lawful, and the expected answer names the cost-justification defense rather than the size of the discount.

terms.definition: The share of contacts answered inside a stated number of seconds, written as a pair — the industry default target is 80% answered within 20 seconds, and the other 20% may wait any length of time at all. That blind spot is why it is reported alongside average speed of answer rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks a competitor to set a staffing target for a holiday peak wants this pair of numbers, not a promise to answer quickly.

terms.definition: A projection of expected future sales based on analysis and historical data.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasts help plan resources and set realistic marketing objectives.

terms.definition: The percentage of total sales in a market captured by one business or product.
terms.whyItMatters: Market share quantifies competitive position and the payoff of a growth strategy.

terms.definition: Employed people divided by the civilian working-age population — the denominator counts everyone of working age, including those not looking for work. With 155 million employed out of 260 million, the ratio is 59.6%; the jobless rate uses the labor force instead and can fall simply because searchers quit looking.
terms.whyItMatters: Unemployment-rate items pair a falling jobless rate with a falling employment share and ask which one shows the labor market actually improving.

terms.definition: Coordinating all promotion for one consistent message across channels.
terms.whyItMatters: Consistency across touchpoints reinforces the message and maximizes impact.

terms.definition: The same offering varies by employee, by customer, and by hour, so quality is a distribution rather than a specification; a factory good is held to a stated tolerance and any unit outside it is scrapped, while service variance has to be squeezed by scripts, training, and blueprints.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on internal service standards is scored on how you narrow the spread between your best and worst shift, not on restating that people differ.

terms.definition: The parliamentary manual whose thresholds get tested: a main motion needs a second and passes on a simple majority of votes cast, an amendment needs a majority, closing debate by moving the previous question needs two-thirds because it takes away a member's right to speak, and a tie fails. Precedence governs order - while an amendment is pending, no new main motion is in order - and a point of order can interrupt because it concerns the rules rather than the question.
terms.whyItMatters: Officer and staff-meeting scenarios ask what vote a motion requires, and the two-thirds threshold for cutting off debate is the one competitors miss.

terms.definition: Share of one cohort of leads that becomes a qualified opportunity: opportunities created divided by the leads that entered in that same period, never by every lead sitting in the database. 40 opportunities from 500 new leads is 8 percent; dividing by a 12,000-record database reports 0.3 percent and hides the follow-up problem entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: Funnel-math items hand you a month of lead counts and opportunity counts and grade the denominator you pick, and a roleplay on tracking prospecting results expects the rate quoted per period rather than against the whole list.

terms.definition: Contacts that disconnect while waiting divided by contacts offered — 90 hang-ups out of 3,000 offered is 3%, and most centers exclude calls dropped inside the first 5 seconds as misdials before reporting it. Under 5% is the common acceptance band, and the number rises non-linearly once average wait passes the caller's patience threshold.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand over the offered and abandoned counts and expect both the percentage and the staffing conclusion drawn from it.

terms.definition: Next period's forecast equals alpha times this period's actual plus (1 minus alpha) times this period's forecast, with alpha between 0 and 1. A high alpha makes the forecast chase recent movement; a low alpha holds it steady, and every past period stays in the number at a shrinking weight.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting questions give last period's forecast, its actual and a smoothing constant and expect one number back; they also ask which alpha suits a volatile category, which is a judgment the formula makes visible.

terms.definition: A brand architecture in which the corporate name stays off the products and each brand carries its own separate equity — Procter & Gamble's Tide, Pampers and Gillette show no visible parent — which is the opposite of a branded house, where one master name fronts every offering; the trade-off is that a failure in one brand cannot contaminate the others, paid for by funding awareness separately for each name.
terms.whyItMatters: Corporate-branding roleplays ask whether a new line should carry the parent name; the answer turns on this architecture choice and the contamination risk it prices.

terms.definition: The process by which unclaimed property — uncashed payroll checks, dormant customer credits, and in some states unused gift-card balances — reverts to the state after a statutory dormancy period, typically three to five years. Holders must attempt due-diligence outreach to the owner and file annual reports, so the balance is a liability to remit rather than a windfall the business gets to book as income.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about years of outstanding checks on a bank reconciliation ask who is legally entitled to that money.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.definition: The Media Rating Council standard that counts a display impression only when at least 50% of its pixels hold the screen for one continuous second — two continuous seconds for video — so a campaign can serve 1,000,000 impressions and have only 600,000 of them count.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay where the client is billed for impressions the audience never had a chance to see is resolved by this standard, and exam items use the gap between served and counted impressions to test whether the competitor knows the threshold.
